touches.text: Machine: tools plus the glue that holds them together. Has an owner. Anything that calls a machine or device, or owns state it must gate, is a machine. Lives inside its device (cairn/devices/<device>/machines/<machine>/), or in cairn/machines/ when several devices hold one (16).

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien until the outline is implemented; a design agent comes after that. Until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, leaving the more capable free for bigger work.
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).
build_inspector
INTENTION:
It outputs only its findings. It certifies nothing, records no crossing, and posts nothing; the gate consumes its findings.

It is the READY TO MERGE ONTO MAIN step of the pipeline: everything's proved, and merging implies pushing it up. With a branch per ticket (3.3.6), commits on the branch are as often as we like; the inspector is the step at ready to merge. Checking what a change touched belongs here; nothing hangs off the git post-commit hook.

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception: that is what the bus is for.

A rule not yet enforced is made into a ticket now, never left floating as prose. So ticket f5dbfddea8c6 makes the rewrites it proposed at the remaining sites (the press office, PROOF.md). Where a site names a rule whose physics is not built, it names that rule's real ticket id, cast now if none exists; the word "ticket" with no id behind it does not count. - CC
Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.
PURPOSE: Python sieves run over a build; reds a component that fails one (no charter, no proofs, a silent device, ...). A new kind of failure found is a new sieve added.
WHY: the inspector does all the checks, so there is no need for more checks anywhere else (17.11.1).
Built with the nest machine (16.2).

A ticket's plan is a plan, not a list of decisions: constraints, outcomes and resources. - Outcomes, not tasks: each is a claim a proof can check. An outcome hides the how. - Constraints: the bounds, and every how Akien is attached to (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel). - Order comes only from real dependencies (you can't test the bus envelope shape until the bus works), and those also set ticket order. - Resources: existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - A plan too big splits into tickets. Early steps can reshape later ones, so the whole is checked for coherence at the end. -amm

The inspectors are not assumed correct; they are examined when they refuse. After a gate refuses, an LLM sets the refusing sieve's intention and why beside the ticket's intention and why and asks: is this sieve the best we can do right now? If yes, the ticket changes. If no, the sieve is fixed through its own ticket and proof. Either way the system improves. WHY: a disagreement becomes an update to an intention or its implementation, never a conversation about procedure. The sieves stay deterministic and never weigh a why; the LLM check comes only after a failure, and it is never a lock pick because it has no third outcome. Nothing passes a ticket over a red.
nest

The reading: - A plan is three parts. Constraints: the bounds, plus every how Akien is attached to, carried verbatim (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel, ...): a how he states is a constraint. Then outcomes. Then resources. - An outcome is {n, claim, writes_to, reads, after: [n or a ticket id], via?}. The claim is falsifiable, one proof tooth per outcome. The falsifier's clauses merge into the outcomes; there is no separate falsifier list. Old clause n stays outcome n; outcomes made from decisions number after them. via (optional) names the tool or pattern to use, drawn from resources. - Order comes from after: only real dependencies, which also shape ticket order. Nothing invents them; list order is reading order only. - Resources: pre-existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - The migration is two steps. Mechanical, on every open ticket now: the plan moves to the new field with clause numbers kept, the trail moves whole to the log, by moves to the log. Judgement, when a ticket is next opened for build, never in bulk: each decision becomes an outcome or a constraint, then a coherence check (every step reads as current; a conflict moves to the log or is named). - CC inference: the mechanical step writes each old decision as an outcome numbered after the clauses, carrying its text and no claim; an outcome with no claim is awaiting judgement and holds BUILDME until the judgement step gives it a claim or moves it to constraints. - akienasus_cc_0 - During the change every reader accepts both shapes. Readers are censused first; one sibling ticket per reader component (RULE 1). - The cast door refuses an outcome with no falsifiable claim, and a plan of more than about 7 outcomes, naming children; each refusal is recorded so the ceiling can be tuned (the 7 is CC's guess). - The [?] markers go. - Tickets: aa3e9a70db47 is the migration (rehearsal); d421051bc1f7 is the hand-built worked example; each reader component has its sibling. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator -amm

WHY: the inspector does all the checks, so there is no need for more checks anywhere else. The inspector's output is consumed by the gate. The gate's output is the certificate. (Akien: the design as meant from the start.)
A ticket cannot call itself a fixit to get the fixit rule: it needs a real red on disk, which code checks.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
